Variance and standard deviation with the right correction, and why

Source: R/spread.R
sprd.Rd

The variance, standard deviation and standard error of the mean of a variable, with the denominator its source calls for: Bessel's \(n - 1\) when the values are a sample from a larger population, \(n\) when they are the whole population and it is being described, and the finite-population correction when they are a sample drawn without replacement from a known, finite population. design = "auto" chooses from N, and the result says which rule it applied and why.

Usage

sprd(
  x,
  des = c("auto", "sample", "census", "finite"),
  N = NULL,
  w = NULL,
  wtype = c("frequency", "reliability"),
  narm = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector.

des

"auto" (default), "sample", "census" or "finite".

N

The population size \(N\), for "finite" and "auto".

w

Optional non-negative weights, one per value.

wtype

"frequency" (default) or "reliability".

narm

Drop missing values (default FALSE: they are an error).

Value

A list of class rmbl_spread: n, mean, variance, sd, semean, design (the rule applied), denominator, and reason (a sentence). The print method shows them.

Details

With \(n\) values \(x_i\) and mean \(\bar x\):

"sample"

values drawn independently from a large population (or from a process). \(s^2 = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 / (n - 1)\) is unbiased for the population variance: the \(n - 1\) (the Bessel correction) makes up for measuring spread around the mean of the sample itself, which is closer to the values than the population mean is. The standard error of the mean is \(s / \sqrt n\).

"census"

every unit of the population is observed (a full count, complete administrative records) and the aim is to describe that population: \(\sigma^2 = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 / n\), with no correction, because \(\bar x\) is the population mean itself; the mean has no sampling error. If the population is instead treated as one realisation of a process (the offences of one year as a draw of what the conditions of the city produce), use "sample".

"finite"

\(n\) units drawn without replacement from \(N\): \(s^2\) (with \(n - 1\)) is unbiased for the population variance defined with \(N - 1\), and the standard error of the mean is \(\sqrt{(1 - n/N) s^2 / n}\); the factor \(1 - n/N\) is the finite-population correction, negligible below a sampling fraction of about 5 percent.

"auto" picks "sample" without N, "census" when \(n = N\), and "finite" when \(n < N\).

With weights: frequency weights (each value stands for \(w_i\) identical observations) use \(\sum w - 1\); reliability or sampling weights (each value counts \(w_i\) times as much) use \(\sum w - \sum w^2 / \sum w\), which is \(n - 1\) when the weights are equal, and the standard error of the weighted mean is the sandwich \(\sqrt{\sum w_i^2 (x_i - \bar x_w)^2} / \sum w_i\). Survey weights from a complex design need the design itself for a standard error (svydes).

References

Cochran WG (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd edition. Wiley, New York, sections 2.4 to 2.6.

See also

svydes for weighted surveys with strata and clusters.

Examples

x <- c(12, 15, 9, 20, 14)
sprd(x)                                   # a sample: n - 1
#> n 5, mean 14, variance 16.5, sd 4.06202, standard error of the mean 1.81659
#> Rule: sample (denominator n - 1 (Bessel)): the values are a sample from a larger population, so the spread is measured around the mean of the sample itself and n - 1 corrects the bias that causes.
sprd(x, des = "census")                # the whole population: n
#> n 5, mean 14, variance 13.2, sd 3.63318, standard error of the mean 0
#> Rule: census (denominator n): the values are the whole population and it is described as it is: the mean is the population mean, so no correction, and the mean has no sampling error.
sprd(x, N = 40)             # 5 of 40 drawn: finite-population correction
#> n 5, mean 14, variance 16.5, sd 4.06202, standard error of the mean 1.69926
#> Rule: finite (denominator n - 1 (Bessel)): 5 of 40 units were drawn without replacement: n - 1 for the variance, and the finite-population correction 1 - n/N = 0.875 for the standard error.
sprd(x, N = 5)              # n = N: a census
#> n 5, mean 14, variance 13.2, sd 3.63318, standard error of the mean 0
#> Rule: census (denominator n): the values are the whole population and it is described as it is: the mean is the population mean, so no correction, and the mean has no sampling error.
sprd(c(1, 2, 3), w = c(10, 5, 1))   # frequency weights
#> n 3, mean 1.4375, variance 0.395833, sd 0.629153, standard error of the mean 0.157288
#> Rule: sample (denominator sum of weights - 1): the values are a sample from a larger population, so the spread is measured around the mean of the sample itself and n - 1 corrects the bias that causes.
